Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**morana** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Morana.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Morana" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Morana" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"morana" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Morana ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Morana ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

### Sacred ​Name

### ‌Winter

​Central ‌domain: ​winter, ‌death.

### ​Living ‌Tradition

### ​Canonical Restoration

​Preserved ‌as ​a ​flagship ‌temple ​with ​its ‌canonical scholarly ​spelling ‌and ​supporting ​evidence.

​The ​domain ‌of ‌winter is ​not ‌a ​modern ​abstraction; ‌it ‌names ‌the ‌sphere of ​influence ‌that ​ancient ​worshippers ​attributed ‌to ​Morana. ​Temples, texts, ​and ‌iconography ​converge ​on ​this ‌sphere, ​even ‌when local ​manifestations ‌differ. ​The ‌PuniCodex ‌restoration ​Morana ​restores ​the name ​that ‌governs ‌the ​domain.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Morana place ‌winter, death ​at the ​center of ​a living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins (Myth)

‌Morana appears ​in slavic ​tradition as ‌winter, death. ​The name's ‌meaning, "Death", ​shapes the ‌narratives told ​about this ​figure.

### Worship ​and Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ​and later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Morana in ‌ritual, text, ​and iconography, ‌ensuring the ​name survived ‌into the ​modern scholarly ‌record.

The ​myths of ​Morana survive ‌in fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later retellings. ​Each version ​reflects the ‌interests of ​its tellers ​— poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not privilege ‌a single ​version; it ​gathers the ​attestations so ​that readers ‌can compare ‌them. The ​restoration Morana ‌gives the ​figure a ​stable name ‌around which ‌these variants ‌orbit.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Morana ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Morana, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​winter ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Morana** ​(*morana*) — ‌Winter, Death ‌· ​The frozen ​goddess of ​endings — ​belongs ​to the ‌Slavic tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Winter, ​Death". The ‌name means ​"Death"[^1].

​**Morana** (Morena, ​Mara, Marzanna) ​is ​the Slavic ‌goddess of ​winter and ‌death ​— the ‌cold season ​and ‌the mortality ​it threatens ‌made ​into a ​single female ‌figure. Where ‌she ‌walks, the ​ground freezes; ​where ‌her effigy ​is drowned ​and burned, ‌the ​thaw begins. ​She is ‌among ​the few ‌Slavic divinities ​whose ​name and ​rite survive ​in attestation ‌from ‌the Middle ​Ages to ‌the ​present day.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Morana** ‌and serves ​its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/morana/). ​The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*morana* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sources.citation: Potebnia, A. A., Obiasneniia malorusskikh i srodnykh narodnykh pesen (Warsaw, 1883) — the earliest philological discussion of the Ukrainian Моренка (Morenka) Kupala songs, in which the drowned maiden is read as an embodiment of death.
Faminzyn, A. S., Bozhestva drevnikh slavian (St Petersburg, 1884) — the first monographic study of the Slavic pantheon, treating Morena/Marzanna on the basis of folk rite rather than written myth.

Kolberg, Oskar, Dzieła wszystkie (Complete Works, 2nd ed. 1961–90), ethnographic volumes on Polish seasonal custom — the principal nineteenth-century documentation of the drowning and burning of the Marzanna effigy.

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Morana** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "Death"[^1].

​The ​canonical ​spelling **Morana** ​matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*morana* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters, ​so no ​lost ‌diacritics ‌or encoding ‌transition ​is ​claimed. The ‌editorial ​work ​is to ‌fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, ​and keep ​the ​original ‌evidence visible. ‌The ​displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ‌computed ‌from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**m** → ​**M** ​— ​Same, capitalized

meditation.body: What ​is remarkable ‌about Morana ‌is not ​what was ​written about ​her ​— almost ​nothing was ‌— but ​what was ​done. A ‌goddess ​with no ‌epic, no ​temple, no ‌priesthood survives ​five centuries ​of ​written history ​because a ​village decided, ‌every year, ​to ‌dress a ​straw doll ‌and drown ​it. The ‌rite is ​her ‌entire biography, ​and it ​is enough. ‌In it ‌we see ‌how ​religion actually ​works: not ‌as doctrine ​but as ​a repeated, ‌embodied ​agreement about ​what time ‌is doing ​to us. ‌Winter arrives, ​winter ​oppresses, winter ​is beautiful ​and lethal, ‌and winter ‌is carried ​to ‌the water ​and drowned ​by the ‌people it ‌starved. Morana ‌teaches ‌that the ​seasons are ‌relationships, not ​weather. She ​is the ​one ‌goddess every ​Slavic child ​meets personally ​— in ‌their ​own hands, ​at their ​own riverbank ‌— and ​she asks ‌the ​oldest question ‌in myth: ​if you ‌cannot banish ‌the cold, ​can ​you at ​least give ​it a ‌face, and ‌drown the ​face?[^1]
